why: With negative values you cannot prune when the running sum exceeds target, so this is really subset enumeration with duplicate skipping: walk sorted values, include or skip each, skip equal values at the same depth, and record any subset whose sum equals target.
hints: In classic Combination Sum II you stop once the sum is too big. Why does that break when negatives exist?
Treat it as generating distinct subsets of a multiset (Subsets II): sort, and at each depth do not start two branches with the same value. Check the sum at every node, not only at leaves.

DFS(start, sum): if sum == target record the path; for i from start, skip if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]; recurse with i + 1. Visiting in sorted order produces the required lexicographic order (shorter prefix first). At most 2^16 nodes.
pitfalls: Record the empty combination only when target == 0, and record matches at every node, since a longer extension may also hit the target (e.g. [-1,1] and [-1,0,1]).
No pruning on sum > target: a later negative can bring it back down.
Duplicate values must not produce duplicate rows; skip equal siblings at the same depth.
